summary:
Recommendation: move the wordpress MySQL database to three AWS services in three waves, with the target schemas designed. Wave 1 moves it 1:1 to Aurora MySQL, which serves 62.6% of the queries. Wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 18 hot reads, covering 81.4% of calls. Wave 3 moves 37.4% of the queries to DynamoDB. The projected cost is $505 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-10-19. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium. Two exposures drive it: data kept in sync between engines by change data capture, and queries where two engines scored almost the same. Test the replication and confirm where those queries run before wave 3 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It moves the database to Aurora MySQL, the same engine family as MySQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source.

risks.description: [dynamodb] The DynamoDB schema design records 25 trade-offs to review; each one is in the engineering report.
details: Comments and their metadata share one item collection keyed by comment_id. The COMMENT item has the sort key COMMENT and each metadata item has the sort key META# followed by meta_id zero-padded to 20 digits

Datetime columns are stored as ISO 8601 strings. MySQL zero dates (0000-00-00 00:00:00), the default for several columns, have no valid ISO 8601 form, so the migration omits the attribute for those rows instead of writing a string

DynamoDB has no auto-increment column. The inserts `445ec39b`, `126679dc`, `2caa2be1` and `7ead756f` write items keyed on a numeric ID that MySQL assigned. The writer now allocates that ID, and each PutItem carries `attribute_not_exists` on the partition key. The migration loads the existing IDs unchanged

Large text columns stay inline: comment_content (item average 552 bytes), commentmeta.meta_value (average 52,429 bytes), api_keys.nonces (average 52,429 bytes) and the action log message (item average 168 bytes). The source row size figures come from the table size divided by the row count

Queries `2c0093ed` and `33dfdb12` add to and subtract from wp_postmeta.meta_value. The column is a string, so DynamoDB stores it as S and cannot apply an atomic ADD to it. The application reads the value, computes the new one and writes it back

Query `3440484f` reads a post by ID and post_type. GetItem cannot filter, so it reads the item by post_id and the application compares post_type. The ORDER BY post_date has no effect because the ID selects one row
Query `3a74580e` reads several users in one SQL IN list; DynamoDB serves it as one Query per user_id, each in umeta_id order

Reads use eventually consistent GetItem, BatchGetItem and Query on the base tables. The partition keys wp_posts, wp_users, wp_termmeta and the meta tables are all base-table keys, so no GSI lag applies

Text columns stay inline in the item: wp_posts averages 711 bytes per row (schema maximum 7526 bytes counting each capped column at 1 KB), wp_postmeta 144, wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta 131 and wp_actionscheduler_actions 587, against the 400 KB item limit. The longtext columns post_content, post_content_filtered, meta_value, schedule and extended_args can each exceed 400 KB in principle

The UPDATE in query `ac34da34` carries attribute_exists(option_name) so it does not create an option that is missing, matching the source UPDATE that affects no row. The upsert in query `a13f5749` is an unconditional PutItem that replaces the whole item

The autoload column is the partition key of the OptionsByAutoload GSI, which serves query `413c99e4` (about 247 rows per call) as a Query on one key value, sorted by option_name. The column has two values in practice, so all indexed items share very few partitions

The comment count of query `8c66eaee` runs as a Query with Select = COUNT on the CommentsByPost index, keyed by comment_post_id with comment_approved as the sort key. The collector has no cardinality statistics for comment_post_id

The consumer_key lookup of query `1794daed` uses the ApiKeysByConsumerKey index, which projects user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces. The last_access update of query `0452bed2` changes an attribute that is not projected

The full read of wp_wc_tax_rate_classes ordered by name (query `329367a2`, 37.9 requests per second at design load) is served by the TaxRateClassesByName index. Every item carries the constant class_scope value ALL as the index partition key, and name is the sort key

The meta tables wp_postmeta, wp_termmeta and wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta use the sort key `meta_key#meta_id`, because WordPress allows several rows with the same owner ID and meta_key. The writes by owner ID and meta_key (queries `ea7778db`, `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`, `3c5c8a79`, `4b856e29`) run as a Query on the owner ID with SK begins_with 'meta_key#', then an UpdateItem per matched item. The same Query serves the term lookup `ee386e4a` and the owner-wide read `50b46567`

The secondary indexes of the source that no query in this group reads are not carried over, such as comment_author_email, comment_parent, comment_date_gmt and the sku, price and stock indexes of wp_wc_product_meta_lookup

The set-based writes of queries `77cd1ad7` (delete reserved stock by order_id) and `2264704d` (update download permissions by order_id) use order_id as the partition key. Each runs as a Query on the order's partition followed by item writes: BatchWriteItem for the delete, UpdateItem per permission for the update

The source auto-increment keys (comment_ID, log_id, meta_id, permission_id, key_id, tax_rate_class_id) and the unique slug of wp_wc_tax_rate_classes have no database-level equivalent in DynamoDB. The inserts of queries `de9a7ba3` and `b05af520` carry attribute_not_exists conditions on their keys

The source indexes on wp_posts (post_author, post_name, post_parent, type_status_date), wp_users (user_login, user_email, user_nicename) and wp_actionscheduler_actions (status, hook, scheduled date, group_id, claim_id) become no GSI, because none of the 20 queries in this group reads by those columns. No source index on these tables is unique apart from the primary key
option_value (longtext) stays inline in the item. The table's avg_row_size_bytes is 360 against the 400 KB item limit, and the schema item size counts the column at 1 KB

wp_options is keyed by option_name instead of the auto-increment option_id, because every lookup, update and delete in queries `66c96f95`, `e223aefb`, `ac34da34`, `a13f5749` and `216d92b3` addresses the option by name

wp_posts, wp_users, wp_termmeta, wp_postmeta, wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta and wp_actionscheduler_actions each become their own DynamoDB table keyed on the entity ID (post_id, user_id, term_id, order_item_id, action_id), because none of the 20 queries in this group joins them

wp_term_relationships keys on post_id (source column object_id) and term_taxonomy_id, so query `0d20f1d9` is a GetItem on the full primary key. The term_taxonomy_id source index has no reader in this group and is not recreated as a GSI
wp_usermeta keeps meta_value inline; the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 16478 against the 400 KB item limit, and meta_value is counted at 1 KB in the 1328-byte schema item size

trade_offs.description: Types carry over one to one from the MySQL source; the only schema changes are index changes driven by the hot queries.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs no code changes for types, and migration risk stays low. Gains come from fewer rows examined per query, at the cost of slightly more storage and write work for three extra or reordered indexes.

trade_offs.description: Comments and their metadata share one item collection keyed by comment_id. The COMMENT item has the sort key COMMENT and each metadata item has the sort key META# followed by meta_id zero-padded to 20 digits.
trade_offs.impact: Reading a comment's metadata is one Query on the comment's partition, with no join. The padding keeps the sort order equal to the source ORDER BY meta_id. The source IN list over several comment ids becomes one Query per id, so query `65f7884e` issues as many requests as it lists ids.

trade_offs.description: The comment count of query `8c66eaee` runs as a Query with Select = COUNT on the CommentsByPost index, keyed by comment_post_id with comment_approved as the sort key. The collector has no cardinality statistics for comment_post_id.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB bills a count for every index entry it reads (about 100 bytes per KEYS_ONLY entry, 1 MB per page), so the cost grows with the number of comments on a post. If a post collects many comments, an atomic counter item updated in the same transaction as the comment write replaces the count query. The index is eventually consistent: a count includes a new comment once DynamoDB has applied the write to the index, and the base table offers no strongly consistent count.

trade_offs.description: The full read of wp_wc_tax_rate_classes ordered by name (query `329367a2`, 37.9 requests per second at design load) is served by the TaxRateClassesByName index. Every item carries the constant class_scope value ALL as the index partition key, and name is the sort key.
trade_offs.impact: The read is a Query instead of a Scan and returns the classes in name order. All items sit in one index partition, which is safe for a table of 2 items of about 447 bytes at 19 read units per second against the 3,000 limit. New classes must be written with class_scope set to ALL.

trade_offs.description: The consumer_key lookup of query `1794daed` uses the ApiKeysByConsumerKey index, which projects user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces. The last_access update of query `0452bed2` changes an attribute that is not projected.
trade_offs.impact: The authentication path is one Query with no second read. The 248.3 last_access updates per second at design load cost 2 write units each against the base table only, so they cause no index writes. The index is eventually consistent: a new or rotated key is found once DynamoDB has applied it to the index. A caller that must see a key it just created reads the base item by key_id with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: The set-based writes of queries `77cd1ad7` (delete reserved stock by order_id) and `2264704d` (update download permissions by order_id) use order_id as the partition key. Each runs as a Query on the order's partition followed by item writes: BatchWriteItem for the delete, UpdateItem per permission for the update.
trade_offs.impact: Neither write scans a table. The multi-row statement is no longer atomic: if the application fails between item writes, some items of the order are changed and the rest are not, and a retry of the same write completes it because each write is idempotent. A caller needing all-or-nothing behavior wraps the items of one order in TransactWriteItems, which accepts up to 100 items.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: comment_content (item average 552 bytes), commentmeta.meta_value (average 52,429 bytes), api_keys.nonces (average 52,429 bytes) and the action log message (item average 168 bytes). The source row size figures come from the table size divided by the row count.

trade_offs.impact: Each user meta row stays one item, so query `3a74580e` reads a user's meta in one Query. A value that grows toward 400 KB would have to move to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: wp_woocommerce_order_items is keyed by order_id and order_item_id, and the application generates order_item_id because DynamoDB has no auto-increment. order_item_name stays inline: the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 129 against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: wp_term_relationships keys on post_id (source column object_id) and term_taxonomy_id, so query `0d20f1d9` is a GetItem on the full primary key. The term_taxonomy_id source index has no reader in this group and is not recreated as a GSI.

trade_offs.description: wp_options is keyed by option_name instead of the auto-increment option_id, because every lookup, update and delete in queries `66c96f95`, `e223aefb`, `ac34da34`, `a13f5749` and `216d92b3` addresses the option by name.

trade_offs.description: The autoload column is the partition key of the OptionsByAutoload GSI, which serves query `413c99e4` (about 247 rows per call) as a Query on one key value, sorted by option_name. The column has two values in practice, so all indexed items share very few partitions.

trade_offs.description: option_value (longtext) stays inline in the item. The table's avg_row_size_bytes is 360 against the 400 KB item limit, and the schema item size counts the column at 1 KB.

trade_offs.description: The UPDATE in query `ac34da34` carries attribute_exists(option_name) so it does not create an option that is missing, matching the source UPDATE that affects no row. The upsert in query `a13f5749` is an unconditional PutItem that replaces the whole item.

trade_offs.description: Options are cached as one hash per option_name with a one-hour TTL.
trade_offs.impact: After a settings change the cached option stays until the owner write path deletes its key, and for at most the one-hour TTL if that delete fails. A read that must see the change at once reads the owner database, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: Post meta and order item meta are stored as one hash per parent, with meta_key as the field.
trade_offs.impact: A batched IN-list read becomes one pipelined HGETALL per ID instead of one query. Duplicate meta_key rows on the same parent collapse into one field, so the application must treat repeated keys as a single value or store them as a list in that field. Each hash is bounded to under 100 KB.

trade_offs.description: Terms are denormalized: wp_terms and wp_term_taxonomy rows share one hash per term, and an object's terms are a set of taxonomy:term_id members.
trade_offs.impact: A denormalized term entry is rebuilt by the write that changes either source row; a read that must see that change before the rebuild reads the owner database, which serves every cache miss. The captured workload has no term write, so staleness is bounded by the one-hour and 30-minute TTLs.

trade_offs.description: Scheduler lookups use short TTLs of 30 and 60 seconds.
trade_offs.impact: A newly scheduled action or a status change is visible to cached reads after at most 60 seconds. The cache absorbs repeated lookups within that window, and the owner database serves every miss and every write.

trade_offs.description: Two post queries stay with the owner database: the four-table term join with an arithmetic sort and the SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS listing.
trade_offs.impact: These reads (query `4481cc0c` and query `d4bf16d6`) get no cache benefit and keep their current latency and load on the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: The query joins four tables, filters on a taxonomy list and an object list, and sorts by an arithmetic expression on a term meta value. The result depends on every input list, so there is no stable key to cache it under.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Build the list from the wp_term_relationships:{object_id}:terms and wp_terms:{term_id} keys and sort in the application, or read the owner database.

unsupported_patterns.reason: The query pages a post listing with SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS and a variable offset, and every observed call returned zero rows, so a cache has nothing to hold.
unsupported_patterns.workaround: Serve it from the owner database.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: Application code keeps issuing the paged post listing to the owner database; no Redis command replaces the total-count step.

The application reads the cache key first, fills it from the owner database on a miss with the TTL set in the key design, and deletes or updates the key in the same code path that performs the owner write.

trade_offs.description: Types carry over one to one from the MySQL source; the only schema changes are index changes driven by the hot queries.
trade_offs.impact: The application needs no code changes for types, and migration risk stays low. Gains come from fewer rows examined per query, at the cost of slightly more storage and write work for three extra or reordered indexes.

trade_offs.description: Comments and their metadata share one item collection keyed by comment_id. The COMMENT item has the sort key COMMENT and each metadata item has the sort key META# followed by meta_id zero-padded to 20 digits.
trade_offs.impact: Reading a comment's metadata is one Query on the comment's partition, with no join. The padding keeps the sort order equal to the source ORDER BY meta_id. The source IN list over several comment ids becomes one Query per id, so query `65f7884e` issues as many requests as it lists ids.

trade_offs.description: The comment count of query `8c66eaee` runs as a Query with Select = COUNT on the CommentsByPost index, keyed by comment_post_id with comment_approved as the sort key. The collector has no cardinality statistics for comment_post_id.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB bills a count for every index entry it reads (about 100 bytes per KEYS_ONLY entry, 1 MB per page), so the cost grows with the number of comments on a post. If a post collects many comments, an atomic counter item updated in the same transaction as the comment write replaces the count query. The index is eventually consistent: a count includes a new comment once DynamoDB has applied the write to the index, and the base table offers no strongly consistent count.

trade_offs.description: The full read of wp_wc_tax_rate_classes ordered by name (query `329367a2`, 37.9 requests per second at design load) is served by the TaxRateClassesByName index. Every item carries the constant class_scope value ALL as the index partition key, and name is the sort key.
trade_offs.impact: The read is a Query instead of a Scan and returns the classes in name order. All items sit in one index partition, which is safe for a table of 2 items of about 447 bytes at 19 read units per second against the 3,000 limit. New classes must be written with class_scope set to ALL.

trade_offs.description: The consumer_key lookup of query `1794daed` uses the ApiKeysByConsumerKey index, which projects user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces. The last_access update of query `0452bed2` changes an attribute that is not projected.
trade_offs.impact: The authentication path is one Query with no second read. The 248.3 last_access updates per second at design load cost 2 write units each against the base table only, so they cause no index writes. The index is eventually consistent: a new or rotated key is found once DynamoDB has applied it to the index. A caller that must see a key it just created reads the base item by key_id with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: The set-based writes of queries `77cd1ad7` (delete reserved stock by order_id) and `2264704d` (update download permissions by order_id) use order_id as the partition key. Each runs as a Query on the order's partition followed by item writes: BatchWriteItem for the delete, UpdateItem per permission for the update.
trade_offs.impact: Neither write scans a table. The multi-row statement is no longer atomic: if the application fails between item writes, some items of the order are changed and the rest are not, and a retry of the same write completes it because each write is idempotent. A caller needing all-or-nothing behavior wraps the items of one order in TransactWriteItems, which accepts up to 100 items.
